teaser: One sentence has just been spoken. Leonardo paints the second after.

lesson.text: “One of you will betray me.” The sentence has just left Jesus's mouth. Nobody has had time to answer. What Leonardo paints is the second that follows: twelve friends at dinner, hit by the same words at the same moment.

Earlier painters showed this meal as a quiet row of saints. Leonardo wanted a room in uproar. He studied how real people take bad news and listed gestures in his notebooks: a man turning with a knife still in his hand, another showing his open palms, another bending to whisper in his neighbor's ear.

lesson.title: The shock wave
lesson.text: The twelve apostles split into four groups of three. Follow the news as it travels along the table.

spots.title: The far left
spots.text: At the end of the table, Bartholomew has jumped to his feet and leans on both hands, straining to hear. Two seats along, Andrew lifts both palms: not me.

spots.title: Beside Jesus
spots.text: Thomas pushes a raised finger forward. James throws his arms wide and pulls back. Behind them Philip presses both hands to his chest, as if asking: surely you don't mean me?

spots.title: The far right
spots.text: Too far away to be sure of what they heard, the last three turn to each other. The man in blue points both hands back toward Jesus while his face questions his neighbors.

lesson.text: In the middle of this storm, one figure does not move. Jesus sits with his arms open and his eyes lowered. And one group was missing from that tour: the three men seated just to the left of him as you face the wall. The traitor is among them.

Painters before Leonardo made Judas easy to spot. They sat him alone on the near side of the table, with his back to the viewer. Leonardo puts him in the row with everyone else. To catch him, you have to read bodies.
Which of these men is Judas? Tap him.

spots.title: Judas
spots.text: He recoils, and his face drops into shadow: the only dark face at the table. His elbow rests on the cloth and his right hand closes around a small purse, the price of the betrayal.

lesson.text: Behind him, grey-haired Peter lunges toward young John to whisper something, and pushes Judas forward as he does. Guilt, anger and sorrow are packed into a single knot of three heads. Nobody in the room has noticed the guilty man yet. You have.

The prior of the convent complained that the painter was taking forever. According to the writer Vasari, Leonardo replied that he was still searching for a face wicked enough for Judas, and that if pressed, he could always use the prior's.

This picture is not on canvas. It covers the end wall of a dining hall, the refectory of the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, and it is enormous: about 4.6 by 8.8 meters (15 by 29 feet). The Duke of Milan, Ludovico Sforza, ordered it around 1495. The friars ate below it, as if Jesus's table were one more table in their own room.

To make the wall seem to open onto a second room, Leonardo used perspective: a way of drawing in which parallel edges shrink toward a single point, so a flat surface looks deep. Where he placed that point is no accident.
Trace the edges of the painted room and see where they lead.

lines.label: Left wall
lines.text: The tops of the dark wall hangings step down toward the back of the room. Extend that slope and it keeps going, straight to one spot.

lines.label: Right wall
lines.text: The same happens on this side. Both lines meet at Jesus's head. Every edge of the architecture points at him.

lines.label: A still triangle
lines.text: His head and open arms draw a triangle, a shape that sits firmly on its base. Around him bodies twist and lean. He alone is at rest.

lesson.text: Restorers found a small hole in the plaster at Jesus's temple. Leonardo seems to have driven a nail there and stretched strings from it to rule the lines of his perspective.
Leonardo turned a holy scene into human drama: one sentence, thirteen reactions, and a room in which every line leads to the calm man at the center.

Now the bad news. Wall paintings were normally done in fresco: color brushed onto wet plaster, which locks it in as it dries. Fresco demands speed. Leonardo liked to hesitate and retouch. A boy who lived at the convent later recalled him painting from dawn to dusk without eating, then staying away for days. So he worked on a dry wall, with a mix of tempera and oil of his own devising.

The experiment failed. The paint never bonded with the damp wall and began to flake within about twenty years, while Leonardo was still alive. By the middle of the 1500s visitors described a blur of stains. Much of what you see is what survived, patiently cleaned by restorers between 1978 and 1999.
People were not always gentle with it either. Wander over the wall and you will find one brutal scar, along with a few details that made it through five centuries.

spots.title: The door
spots.text: In 1652 the friars enlarged a doorway in this wall. It sliced through the bottom of the painting and took Jesus's feet with it. They are lost for good.

spots.title: Three windows
spots.text: Openings onto blue hills. The middle one sits right behind Jesus's head and frames it with daylight: a natural halo instead of a golden disc.

spots.title: Thomas's finger
spots.text: A raised index finger. Thomas is the apostle who, in the Gospel, will later ask to touch Jesus's wounds before he believes.

spots.title: Peter's knife
spots.text: A hand bent backward at the hip holds a knife. It is Peter's. Later that night, in the garden, he will draw a blade to defend Jesus.

spots.title: Bread and wine
spots.text: Jesus's hands open toward the bread and the wine on the table. This supper is also the origin of Communion, the Christian rite of sharing both.

spots.title: The tablecloth
spots.text: Blue woven bands and crisp fold lines, as if the linen had just been taken from a chest. Leonardo painted the cloth of an ordinary, well-kept table.

lesson.text: The worst came in August 1943, when an Allied bomb struck the convent. The roof of the refectory and one of its long walls collapsed. Leonardo's wall, shielded by sandbags and scaffolding, was left standing among the rubble, open to the sky.

The refectory is now a sealed, climate-controlled room. Visitors enter in small groups and may stay fifteen minutes. That is about how long the scene itself would last before someone finally answered.

quiz.question: What moment of the supper does Leonardo show?
options: The second after Jesus announces a betrayal
The apostles arriving at the table
quiz.explanation: The painting shows the reactions right after “One of you will betray me.”

quiz.question: How did Leonardo make Judas different from earlier versions?
options: He sat him in the row with the others, his face in shadow
He placed him alone on the near side of the table
He left him out of the picture
quiz.explanation: Earlier painters isolated Judas. Leonardo hides him in a group and marks him with shadow.

quiz.question: Where do the perspective lines of the room meet?
quiz.explanation: The slopes of both walls converge on Jesus's head.

quiz.question: Why did the painting start flaking so early?
options: It was painted on canvas glued to the wall
Leonardo painted on dry plaster with an experimental mix instead of true fresco
The friars washed it every year
quiz.explanation: His tempera and oil mix never bonded with the damp wall.

quiz.question: What happened to Jesus's feet?
options: They were cut away when a doorway was enlarged in 1652
They were destroyed by the 1943 bomb
quiz.explanation: The friars enlarged a door through the bottom of the painting.

facts.text: The Last Supper is a true fresco, painted on wet plaster.
facts.explanation: Leonardo painted on a dry wall with tempera and oil, which is why it deteriorated so fast.

facts.text: The apostles are arranged in four groups of three.
facts.explanation: Leonardo bundles the twelve into four trios, two on each side of Jesus.

facts.text: The painted wall collapsed in the bombing of 1943 and was rebuilt.
facts.explanation: The roof and a side wall fell, but Leonardo's wall, protected by sandbags, stayed standing.
